0001 | UPDATE: Misha Lavrov (see comments) has convinced me this proposed solution is incorrect. I have shown there exist a $4-$colouring of $G$ in which $\partial(G)$  requires $3-$colours. However this result together with the knowledge that there exist a $3-$ colouring of $\overline{G}$ is not sufficient to show that $G$ is $3-$colourable. In particular just because "two-parts" of the graph require only $3$ colours this will not imply the whole graph requires only $3$ colours. 
0002 | 
0003 | 
0004 | ----------
0005 | 
0006 | 
0007 | If $U$ is the unit disc centered at the origin consider $n$ chords drawn through the interior of $U$ such that no two chords are parallel and no three chords intersect at the same point. The arrangement graph $G$ induced by the discs and the chords has a vertex for each intersection point in the interior of $U$ and $2$ vertices for each chord incident to the boundary of $U.$ Naturally $G$ has an edge for each arc directly connecting two intersection points. $G$ is planar and $3-$connected.
0008 | 
0009 | 
0010 | ----------
0011 | 
0012 | >***Question:*** Can we show that $\chi(G)=3$ ?
0013 | 
0014 | ----------
0015 | 
0016 | Proposed Solution (2019):
0017 | 
0018 | In this post the terms points and vertices are used interchangeably. As well as those of arcs and edges. I use $\chi()$ to denote the vertex colouring of a graph. All colourings are assumed to be proper. I write the following:
0019 | 
0020 |  1. $\overline{G}$ - for the arrangement graph induced by the simple arrangement of chords drawn in the interior of $U.$ Note $\overline{G}$ does not have any edges incident to the boundary of $U.$
0021 |  2. $\partial{G}$ - for the $2n$-cycle induced by the vertices and arcs along the boundary of $U.$
0022 |  3. $G+x$ - for the one-point-extended graph of $G.$ That is a point $x$ which is exterior to the boundary of $U$ with a line drawn from every point on the boundary of $U$ to $x.$
0023 | 
0024 | Observe that $\chi(G)>2$ as $G$ contains $3-$cycles (or triangles). It is known that $\chi(\overline{G})=3.$ This fact was established by Felsner, Hurtado, Noy and Streinu in 2006 by way of wiring diagrams. It suffices to show that $\chi(\partial G)=3$ is order to establish that $G$ is $3-$colourable. 
0025 | 
0026 | Consider $G+x.$ Observe that $G+x$ is planar and so by the $4-$colour theorem we have that $\chi(G+x)=4.$  If $\chi(\partial{G})=4$ then the point $x$ would have to be a colour that is different than any of the $4$ colours applied to the points on $\partial G.$ In particular $x$ would require a fifth colour and so $G+x$ would be $5$-colourable - a contradiction. And so $\chi(\partial{G})\leq 3$ and consequently $G$ is $3$-colourable. This completes the solution $\blacksquare.$
0027 |
